advice.scenario: Your child wants a later weekend bedtime and has good reasons.
advice.guidance: You already explain your rules, so let your child propose the plan this time: how much later, and how they'll catch up on sleep. Post it where everyone can see it and review it together after a month.
advice.challenge: This week, let your child lead on setting one sleep rule.

advice.scenario: Your child says all their friends can game until ten.
advice.guidance: Name the feeling first: "Being compared isn't fun." Then check together whether the rule still fits. As your child grows, hand over screen management step by step, with check-ins instead of daily watching.
advice.challenge: Agree on a one-week screen-time self-management trial.

advice.scenario: Grades are steady, but your child has lost interest in one subject.
advice.guidance: Ask "What makes this subject hard to care about?" before explaining why it matters. Agree on one small goal, such as bringing one confusing question home each week to talk through.
advice.challenge: Ask one open question about school each day, and just listen.

advice.scenario: Your child wants to go somewhere with friends that you don't know well.
advice.guidance: Make your worries specific: who's going, when they'll be home, how to reach them. Ask your child for a plan that puts you at ease, and keep your word once you agree.
advice.challenge: This week, let your child write the safety plan for one outing.

advice.scenario: Your child agreed to take out the trash but always needs reminding.
advice.guidance: Find out together whether it's the task or the timing that doesn't work. Swapping the chore or the time is fine, as long as you agree on a way it gets done without you, such as a phone reminder.
advice.challenge: Let your child pick one chore and own it for a whole week.

advice.scenario: Your child comes home from an exam and says nothing.
advice.guidance: Skip the score for now and say, "You look tired. I'm here when you want to talk." When they open up, repeat back what they feel before planning next steps together.
advice.challenge: Three times this week, just listen without giving advice.

advice.scenario: Your child wants to spend pocket money on something you think is a waste.
advice.guidance: Share your view, then leave the decision to them. If they regret it, that's a great lesson. Talk it over afterwards instead of saying "I told you so."
advice.challenge: Make a one-month pocket money plan together.

advice.scenario: Your child contradicts you in front of guests.
advice.guidance: Stay calm in the moment and talk in private later. Acknowledge that they have their own view, and say how you'd like disagreements to be expressed.
advice.challenge: This week, invite your child to tell you where they disagree.

advice.scenario: Your child wants to stay up late revising during exam week.
advice.guidance: Recognise the effort first, then weigh it up together: extra revision hours against a clear head tomorrow. Let your child set a latest time, and remind them only once when it arrives.
advice.challenge: During exam week, remind only once at the agreed time each night.

advice.scenario: Your child goes to bed on time but scrolls in bed before sleeping.
advice.guidance: Ask how they sleep after scrolling, instead of announcing a new rule. Invite them to suggest a fix, such as charging phones in the living room, and do it yourself too.
advice.challenge: This week, every phone in the family stays outside the bedroom overnight.

advice.scenario: Your child wants to download a social app you don't know.
advice.guidance: Ask your child to show you the app: how it works, who can see their posts, what to do if a stranger messages them. Set the privacy options together and agree that they'll tell you if anything feels wrong.
advice.challenge: This week, ask your child to teach you one app they use often.

advice.scenario: You often check your phone while your child is talking to you.
advice.guidance: Rules apply to adults too. When your child starts talking, put your phone face down and say, "Go on, I'm listening." Your example makes later talks about screens more convincing.
advice.challenge: Each time your child talks to you this week, put your phone down first.

advice.scenario: Your child wants to quit an after-school class.
advice.guidance: Ask "Which part makes you want to stop?" to find out whether it's tiredness, lost interest or trouble with people there. You could agree to keep going until a set point, such as the end of term, and then let your child decide.
advice.challenge: Agree on a date when your child will decide whether to continue.

advice.scenario: Your child does well at school, but you notice you ask about marks more and more.
advice.guidance: Swap the question for "What was the most interesting thing you learned today?" Focusing on the process helps your child feel learning is theirs, not something done to please you.
advice.challenge: This week, don't ask about marks; each day ask what was interesting instead.

advice.scenario: Your child wants to plan their own revision without you checking.
advice.guidance: Try letting go, and agree on one check-in you're both happy with, such as ten minutes on Sunday looking at the plan together. If it goes well, loosen it further.
advice.challenge: This week, look at the study plan only at the agreed time.

advice.scenario: Your child has fallen out with a close friend and is upset.
advice.guidance: Start with "It sounds like this friendship really matters to you," and hold off on judging who was right. Once they're calmer, ask what they want to do, and only give advice if they ask.
advice.challenge: When your child talks about friends this week, ask "Do you want advice, or just to talk?"

advice.scenario: Your child wants to invite friends over.
advice.guidance: Say yes warmly and agree on the details together: how many, when it ends, which rooms are fine. Let your child handle the tidy-up afterwards; it's practice at being a host.
advice.challenge: Plan one visit from friends together this week and let your child handle the clean-up.

advice.scenario: Your child says chores are unfair because a younger sibling does less.
advice.guidance: Take the complaint seriously: ask your child to list every household job, then look at the split together. Adjusting by age is fine, but explain why, and agree to review it regularly.
advice.challenge: Make a family chore chart together this week and put it up.

advice.scenario: Your child says they want to learn to cook.
advice.guidance: Make the most of it: give them one dish a week, from shopping to clean-up. Be the helper, not the chef, and step in only for safety.
advice.challenge: Let your child cook one dish for a family meal this week.

advice.scenario: Your child raises their voice at you when they're upset.
advice.guidance: Stay calm and say, "I want to hear this. Let's both take five minutes and then talk." Afterwards, respond to the feeling first, then say how you'd like it expressed next time.
advice.challenge: This week, suggest a five-minute pause once when an argument heats up.

advice.scenario: You had a bad day and snapped at your child.
advice.guidance: Go back and say, "I had a bad day and I was short with you. I'm sorry." When you show how to handle your own feelings, your child learns to do the same.
advice.challenge: If you snap at your child this week, apologise the same day.

advice.scenario: Your child wants to earn some money, for example by walking a neighbour's dog.
advice.guidance: Show support first, then look at a few things together: whether it affects school and sleep, whether it's safe, and what the money is for. Agree on a trial period and review it together.
advice.challenge: Write down one earning or saving goal with your child this week.

advice.scenario: Your child runs out of pocket money halfway through the month.
advice.guidance: Don't top it up straight away; look together at where the money went. Try paying weekly, or splitting it into "spend" and "save", then see how next month goes.
advice.challenge: Ask your child to note their spending each day this week, and look at it together at the weekend.

advice.scenario: Your child shuts their door and doesn't want you walking in.
advice.guidance: Knock and wait for an answer. Respect their space, while explaining when you'll need to come in, such as for safety or something you agreed. Children whose privacy is respected open the door more often.
advice.challenge: Knock and wait every time before entering your child's room this week.

advice.scenario: When the family makes a decision, your child says "You'll decide anyway."
advice.guidance: Respond seriously: "Your view matters to us. You go first this time." Pick one decision that affects them and actually use their idea, so they see that speaking up counts.
advice.challenge: This week, let your child speak first on one family decision and use one of their ideas.

advice.scenario: Your child asks to stay up later, you say "No," and they slam their door.
advice.guidance: Start with "What do you want the extra time for?" The rule can stay, but listen first and then explain why, such as how sleep affects the next day. Children who feel heard are more willing to follow rules.
advice.challenge: This week, add "because…" every time you set a rule.

advice.scenario: You take your child's phone and they say you're being unfair.
advice.guidance: Before taking it, say which agreement was broken and when and how they can get it back. The clearer and more predictable the consequence, the less it feels personal.
advice.challenge: Write down the screen rules and consequences together.

advice.scenario: Your child scores 85 and your first question is "What about the other 15?"
advice.guidance: Start with the effort and progress, then ask what they think could be better. Goals your child names themselves motivate more than goals you hand them.
advice.challenge: This week, open every talk about grades with something that went well.

advice.scenario: You don't like one of your child's friends and ban them from meeting.
advice.guidance: Find out what your child likes about this friend, then name the specific behaviour that worries you. Instead of a ban, agree on situations where your child will tell you or leave.
advice.challenge: Ask your child to tell you about a friend. Only ask, don't judge.

advice.scenario: Your child is slow with a chore, so you take over, annoyed.
advice.guidance: Explain the standard you expect, show it once, and then let go. Say thank you even if it isn't perfect, and improve one detail together.
advice.challenge: This week, say thank you before giving any feedback on chores.

advice.scenario: Your child cries and you say "Crying won't help."
advice.guidance: Feelings aren't misbehaviour. Try "You're really upset right now, aren't you?" and wait until they're calm to talk about the problem. Children who feel understood recover faster.
advice.challenge: This week, name your child's feeling first whenever they're upset.

advice.scenario: Your child asks for pocket money and you say money isn't their business.
advice.guidance: Teenagers need practice managing money. Give a small, fixed amount, say which costs are theirs to cover, and let them learn from small mistakes.
advice.challenge: Talk through one real household expense with your child.

advice.scenario: Your child talks back and you say "I'm your parent, so you listen."
advice.guidance: Being the parent isn't a reason. Once you're both calm, say which way of talking hurts you, and ask how your child would like you to talk to them. Respect goes both ways.
advice.challenge: If you speak too harshly this week, apologise once.

advice.scenario: Your child is ten minutes late to bed and you want to cancel their weekend plans.
advice.guidance: Pause and ask yourself whether the consequence fits the problem. Try "You were late tonight, so let's be on time tomorrow." Small slips with small consequences make rules feel fair.
advice.challenge: Before setting any consequence this week, check that it fits the problem.

advice.scenario: You set the sleep routine but have never asked your child whether it works.
advice.guidance: At a calm moment ask, "What's the hardest part of the current routine for you?" You don't have to change everything, but adjust one thing so your child sees their view counts.
advice.challenge: Adjust one part of the routine this week based on your child's input.

advice.scenario: You worry about online safety and want to check your child's phone whenever you like.
advice.guidance: Tell your child exactly what worries you, such as strangers, scams or harmful content. Agree together on when and how you'll look at their phone. An open agreement makes them more likely to come to you when something goes wrong than surprise checks do.
advice.challenge: This week, talk about online safety once and agree on one rule for phone checks.

advice.scenario: You call your child while they're gaming, they don't stop at once, and you shout.
advice.guidance: Many games can't be paused instantly. Try a five-minute warning: "Dinner in five minutes." A little notice gets better results than an instant order.
advice.challenge: Give a five-minute warning every time you need your child off a screen this week.

advice.scenario: Your child hasn't finished their homework, so you ban them from going out.
advice.guidance: First find out where it's stuck: too hard, too much, or being put off? Work on that cause together, such as tackling the hardest question first. Solving the problem gets homework done more reliably than punishment.
advice.challenge: When homework stalls this week, first ask "Where are you stuck?"

advice.scenario: You chose your child's subjects or activities for them.
advice.guidance: Share your reasons, then ask what your child would choose and why. You could meet halfway: one option you suggest, one they decide. Children try harder at things they chose.
advice.challenge: This week, hear your child's view on one choice before giving yours.

advice.scenario: Your child asks to go to a classmate's birthday party and your first reaction is no.
advice.guidance: Hold off and say, "Let me think. Tell me more first." Ask when, where and whether an adult will be there. A yes with conditions is often safer than a flat no, because your child keeps being honest with you.
advice.challenge: This week, ask for details before answering any request from your child.

advice.scenario: You want your child to call every hour when they're out with friends.
advice.guidance: Safety matters, but too many check-ins feel like distrust. Agree on a message when they arrive and when they leave, plus a call if plans change. If they keep to it, loosen the rules a little.
advice.challenge: Agree this week on how your child checks in when out, and stick to it.

advice.scenario: You hand out chores as orders without saying why.
advice.guidance: Add a reason, such as "If we all tidy up, we can all relax sooner tonight." You can also let your child pick from a few chores. Having a choice means less pushback.
advice.challenge: This week, let your child choose between two chores each time.

advice.scenario: Your child breaks a bowl while washing up.
advice.guidance: Ask "Did you cut yourself?" first, then clean up together. Accidents aren't on purpose and don't need punishing. If every mistake brings a telling-off, children avoid chores or hide problems.
advice.challenge: When your child makes a mistake this week, check on them before the mess.

advice.scenario: Your child says they feel anxious and you reply "What's there to be anxious about?"
advice.guidance: Try "Thanks for telling me. Can you say more?" It takes courage to open up, so take it in first, then work it out together. If the worry keeps affecting daily life, contact the school counsellor.
advice.challenge: When your child shares a worry this week, start with "Thanks for telling me."

advice.scenario: You rarely praise or thank your child.
advice.guidance: Each day, name one specific thing: "Thanks for carrying that," or "You really focused on practice today." Specific praise shows you notice them, and makes your rules easier to accept.
advice.challenge: Say one specific word of praise or thanks to your child every day this week.

advice.scenario: Your child rarely shows their feelings in front of you.
advice.guidance: Share a small feeling of your own first, such as "Work wore me out today." When adults talk about feelings, children learn it's safe to do the same. When they open up, listen without judging.
advice.challenge: Share one of your own feelings with your child each day this week.

advice.scenario: Your child bought something you disagree with using their pocket money, and you want to take it away.
advice.guidance: If it isn't a safety issue, let the decision stand, then talk about whether they'd buy it again. The point of pocket money is practice at choosing, including choosing badly.
advice.challenge: This week, don't interfere with how your child spends their own money; just talk about it afterwards.

advice.scenario: You often say "We can't afford it" to end a request.
advice.guidance: Give a specific reason instead: "Other bills come first this month; let's look again next month." Or explain they can save up for it. Clear reasons help your child understand family choices without needless worry.
advice.challenge: Give a specific reason each time you turn down a spending request this week.

advice.scenario: When your child explains, you interrupt with "No excuses."
advice.guidance: Let them finish before you answer. An explanation isn't an excuse, and you can't respond well until you've heard it. Then say, "I've heard you. My decision is…, because…"
advice.challenge: This week, wait until your child finishes explaining before you speak.

advice.scenario: You often compare your child with other people's children.
advice.guidance: Swap "Look at so-and-so" for "Compared with last time, you…", and only compare your child with their own past. Being compared makes children feel not good enough; seeing their own progress makes them want to keep going.
advice.challenge: Don't compare your child with anyone else this week.

advice.scenario: Your child often stays up past midnight, and saying something feels pointless.
advice.guidance: Agree together on a specific bedtime and where the phone stays at night. Start small, such as 30 minutes earlier. Gentle consistency works better than occasional strictness.
advice.challenge: For five days in a row, remind once at the agreed time and follow through.

advice.scenario: Your child games late into the night and you don't want to spoil the mood.
advice.guidance: Rules don't hurt relationships; inconsistency does. Agree on daily gaming time, give a ten-minute warning, and switch off on time. When you keep to it, your child will adjust.
advice.challenge: Set a daily screen time together this week and stick to it.

advice.scenario: Your child says homework is done and you never check.
advice.guidance: Trust and interest can go together. Once or twice a week, ask your child to tell you what they learned, or look over their homework plan together.
advice.challenge: Twice this week, ask your child to tell you what they learned that day.

advice.scenario: Your child goes out with friends at night and you don't know when they'll be back.
advice.guidance: Agree that before going out, everyone says where, with whom and when they'll be back. It isn't distrust; it's a family safety habit, and you can do it too.
advice.challenge: Try the family "three things" before going out: where, who, when back.

advice.scenario: Your child skips chores and it feels faster to do them yourself.
advice.guidance: Chores teach responsibility. Start with one small daily task, such as clearing the table after dinner. If it isn't done, remind gently, but don't do it for them.
advice.challenge: Give your child one daily chore and don't do it for them this week.

advice.scenario: Whenever your child has a meltdown, you give in.
advice.guidance: You can accept the feeling without changing the answer. Say "I know you're disappointed, and the answer is still no," then stay close until they calm down.
advice.challenge: Once this week, hold a decision kindly while your child is upset.

advice.scenario: You buy your child most things they ask for.
advice.guidance: Try "Let's put it on the wish list and decide next week." Waiting helps your child tell wants from needs and cuts impulse buying.
advice.challenge: Start a wish list together and wait a week before deciding.

advice.scenario: Your child speaks to you rudely and you let it slide.
advice.guidance: You can calmly say "I want to hear you, so please say it another way." Setting a limit teaches your child how to treat people.
advice.challenge: Every time this week, calmly ask your child to rephrase when they're rude.

advice.scenario: Your child begs for "ten more minutes," and it turns into an hour.
advice.guidance: Before agreeing, say, "I'll come back in ten minutes and then it's off." Show up on time, kind but firm. Following through once beats nagging ten times.
advice.challenge: This week, whenever you agree to "ten more minutes," follow through when time is up.

advice.scenario: Your child sleeps until noon at weekends and you don't mind.
advice.guidance: A lie-in now and then is fine, but a big shift makes Mondays hard. Agree on a latest weekend wake-up time, say 10 a.m., and plan something they like for the morning.
advice.challenge: This weekend, wake your child at the agreed time and do something they enjoy together.

advice.scenario: Your child is on their phone throughout meals.
advice.guidance: Suggest a basket where every phone goes during meals, yours included. No lecture needed; just a friendly "Phones in the basket" each time.
advice.challenge: This week, no phones at the table for any family meal.

advice.scenario: Your child plays a game rated above their age, and you avoid saying anything.
advice.guidance: Learn about the game first: look at its age rating and content together. Name exactly what worries you, then look for an alternative, such as a similar game suited to their age. Setting limits is a way of caring.
advice.challenge: This week, check the age rating of a game your child plays, together.

advice.scenario: The rule is "games after homework," but you never check.
advice.guidance: A rule only counts if someone keeps it. Each day spend two minutes asking, "Homework done? Show me the list." Keep it up for a week and it becomes routine.
advice.challenge: Each day this week, check homework is done before screen time starts.

advice.scenario: Your child says they don't want to go to school, and you let them stay home.
advice.guidance: Ask why first: tired, worried about a test, or something happening at school? If it's ordinary reluctance, kindly insist on going. If it involves bullying or feeling unsafe, contact the school straight away.
advice.challenge: This week, when your child resists something they need to do, ask why, then kindly hold firm.

advice.scenario: The day before a test your child starts revising, and you stay up late helping.
advice.guidance: Help this time if you like, but look back afterwards: "How many days earlier next time?" Have your child put the next test in a calendar, and remind them once the week before. Let consequences teach, rather than rescuing every time.
advice.challenge: Put upcoming tests in a calendar with your child this week, with a start date for revision.

advice.scenario: Your child wants to stay out late with friends and you find it hard to say no.
advice.guidance: You can say, "I want you to have fun, and I need you home by ten." Warmth and limits go together. If they complain, acknowledge the disappointment without changing the time.
advice.challenge: Set a time to be home for each outing this week and check they're back on time.

advice.scenario: Your child's friends come over and leave a mess.
advice.guidance: Before the next visit, agree: "Before your friends leave, you all tidy the living room." Remind once at the time, and if it isn't done, your child finishes it. It's a house rule, not a judgment of their friends.
advice.challenge: After any visit from friends this week, your child tidies up.

advice.scenario: You ask for help, your child says "In a minute," and then forgets.
advice.guidance: Turn "In a minute" into a time: "Okay, I'll come back in five minutes." Then ask again and wait nearby until they start. Gentle follow-through builds habits better than doing it yourself.
advice.challenge: When your child says "In a minute" this week, set a time and follow up.

advice.scenario: Your child's room is so messy things get lost, and you keep tidying it for them.
advice.guidance: Stop, and agree on a set time each week when they tidy it themselves while you just remind. You could help set up a few "where things go" spots first, then let them keep it up.
advice.challenge: Don't tidy your child's room this week; only remind them at the agreed time.

advice.scenario: When your child is sad, you buy them something to cheer them up.
advice.guidance: Sit with them first: "Looks like a rough day. Want to talk?" A treat makes the feeling go away for a while, but being heard teaches your child how to handle sadness.
advice.challenge: When your child is upset this week, comfort them with time and listening, not gifts.

advice.scenario: You worry that setting rules will make your child like you less.
advice.guidance: Anger passes; feeling cared for lasts. You can say, "I'm setting this rule because I care about you." They may grumble, but clear limits help children feel secure.
advice.challenge: Keep one rule this week that you'd usually give up on, and say why you care.

advice.scenario: Your child often asks you to top up a game.
advice.guidance: Agree on a monthly game budget that comes out of pocket money. When it's gone, it's gone until next month, with no top-ups. Setting it up front is far easier than haggling each time.
advice.challenge: Set a monthly limit on game spending with your child this week.

advice.scenario: Your child loses something you just bought, and you replace it right away.
advice.guidance: Say "That's a shame" first, then ask your child to pay part of the cost, or wait a while before replacing it. Carrying a little of the cost teaches them to look after their things.
advice.challenge: If your child loses or breaks something this week, let them share the cost.

advice.scenario: Your child takes your things without asking.
advice.guidance: Say calmly, "Ask me before you use my things," and do the same with theirs. Respecting each other's belongings is one of the most basic family rules.
advice.challenge: This week, everyone asks before using someone else's things.

advice.scenario: Your child is rude to a grandparent and you say nothing.
advice.guidance: Afterwards, tell your child privately, "That would have hurt Grandma. Next time you could say…" A specific alternative helps more than "Be polite."
advice.challenge: When your child is rude to family this week, privately suggest a better way to say it.

advice.scenario: You're tired after work and don't know when your child goes to bed.
advice.guidance: You don't need to change much at once. Start by saying good night and asking about tomorrow. Those few minutes tell your child you think about them.
advice.challenge: Say good night to your child every night this week.

advice.scenario: Your child goes straight to their room with their phone and you rarely talk.
advice.guidance: Find one small shared activity, such as watching a video they like and asking why they like it. Knowing your child's world comes before setting rules.
advice.challenge: This week, watch or play one thing your child enjoys, together.

advice.scenario: You're not sure what your child is learning at school now.
advice.guidance: Pick a regular time each week to ask about their favourite and hardest subjects. You don't need to teach; you only need to show interest.
advice.challenge: Ask once this week about your child's favourite and hardest subject.

advice.scenario: You can't name your child's best friend.
advice.guidance: Ask "Who have you been hanging out with? What are they like?" Remember the name and ask about them again; your child will notice you care.
advice.challenge: Learn one friend's name and ask about them next week.

advice.scenario: Everyone at home does their own thing; there's no shared routine.
advice.guidance: Eat one meal together and clear up together for five minutes afterwards. Doing something side by side brings you closer than handing out tasks.
advice.challenge: Plan one household job the whole family does together this week.

advice.scenario: Your child seems unhappy lately and you don't know how to start.
advice.guidance: You can simply say "I've been busy and haven't checked in. How have you really been?" Honesty matters more than technique. If the low mood lasts, contact the school counsellor.
advice.challenge: Find one moment this week to ask "How have you been lately?"

advice.scenario: You give your child money when asked but never ask what it's for.
advice.guidance: Turn it into a conversation: ask what they plan to buy and why they like it. It's an easy way into their interests.
advice.challenge: Next time you give money, spend five minutes talking about what it's for.

advice.scenario: Whatever your child says, you answer with "Mm-hm."
advice.guidance: Look at your child when they talk and respond to one detail, such as "When is that match you mentioned?" Being answered properly is the most basic form of respect.
advice.challenge: Each day this week, respond properly to one thing your child tells you.

advice.scenario: You work late and get home after your child is asleep.
advice.guidance: Send a message before bed: "Hope today went okay. Good night, see you in the morning." Then ask about yesterday at breakfast. Even with little time, your child can feel you're there.
advice.challenge: Send your child a good-night message every day this week.

advice.scenario: Your child often goes to bed very late and is tired at school, and you hadn't noticed.
advice.guidance: Ask, "What time do you usually get to sleep these days?" Find out first, without criticism. Then agree a bedtime together, and go say good night at that time; that itself is a reminder.
advice.challenge: Ask your child once this week when they sleep, and agree a bedtime together.

advice.scenario: After work you're on your phone too, and you and your child each stay on your own screens.
advice.guidance: Set fifteen phone-free minutes a day, such as after dinner. Put yours down first and ask what was fun today. Starting with yourself is easier than asking your child to change.
advice.challenge: Have fifteen phone-free minutes with your child each day this week.

advice.scenario: You find out by chance that your child is online in the middle of the night.
advice.guidance: No need for anger. Start with, "I noticed you were on your phone very late. Couldn't sleep, or is something going on?" Once you know why, agree on one simple rule, such as charging the phone in the living room after 11 p.m.
advice.challenge: Agree where the phone stays overnight, and check it each night this week.

advice.scenario: You rarely read messages and reports from school.
advice.guidance: Pick a set time each week for ten minutes of school messages. When something stands out, mention it: "I saw you've got sports day next week."
advice.challenge: Read the school messages once this week and talk about one item with your child.

advice.scenario: There's a parent-teacher meeting and you'd rather skip it.
advice.guidance: Try to go, or at least contact the teacher. When you show up at school, your child sees their life matters to you. Afterwards, tell them one good thing the teacher said.
advice.challenge: Contact your child's teacher or go to one school event this week.

advice.scenario: Your child mentions trouble with a classmate and you brush it off.
advice.guidance: Stop what you're doing and say, "Sounds annoying. What happened?" Hear the whole story, then ask what help they'd like. If it involves bullying or feeling unsafe, contact the school promptly.
advice.challenge: When your child mentions friends or classmates this week, stop and listen to the end.

advice.scenario: Your child rarely brings friends home.
advice.guidance: Say, "Your friends are welcome here any time," and keep some simple snacks around. A home your child is happy to bring friends to also lets you get to know them naturally.
advice.challenge: Tell your child this week that their friends are welcome, and suggest a time.

advice.scenario: There's no chore plan at home; whoever's free does it.
advice.guidance: Write a simple chart with one or two jobs each, and stick it on the fridge. It doesn't need to be fancy; what matters is that everyone knows their part, you included.
advice.challenge: Make a chore chart this week with one job for each person.

advice.scenario: Your child did a chore and you didn't notice.
advice.guidance: Notice the small things and say, "Thanks for doing the dishes." Effort that gets noticed makes children want to keep going, and helps them feel they belong.
advice.challenge: Thank your child for one thing they did each day this week.

advice.scenario: Your child is crying, you don't know what to say, so you walk away.
advice.guidance: You don't need the right words; just stay nearby. You can say, "I'm not sure how to help, but I'm here." Being there is a comfort in itself.
advice.challenge: When your child is upset this week, sit with them for a while.

advice.scenario: You're under a lot of stress and have no energy left for your child.
advice.guidance: Look after yourself too, and be honest: "I'm really stressed lately. It isn't about you." Then find something low-effort to do together, like a ten-minute walk. If the stress weighs on you for a long time, talk to someone you trust or a professional.
advice.challenge: Do one ten-minute thing with your child each day this week.

advice.scenario: Your child tells you, "You don't even care about me."
advice.guidance: Don't rush to defend yourself. Say, "I'm sad to hear that. Can you tell me when you feel that way?" After listening, pick one thing you can change right away and do it.
advice.challenge: Change one specific habit this week based on what your child told you.

advice.scenario: Your child needs money for school costs, and you often forget.
advice.guidance: Agree on one fixed way, such as your child writing costs on a note on the fridge that you check each evening. Paying on time spares your child awkward moments at school.
advice.challenge: Check your child's note or message each evening this week.

advice.scenario: Your child has no pocket money and has to ask each time they need something.
advice.guidance: Set a small, regular amount and say which costs are theirs. A fixed arrangement means they don't have to ask every time, and they start learning to manage money.
advice.challenge: Agree on a pocket money amount and payday with your child this week.

advice.scenario: You often forget things you promised your child.
advice.guidance: Note promises in your phone as you make them, and if you can't keep one, say so early: "Sorry, I can't make it. How about…?" Keeping your word is the most direct way to show your child respect.
advice.challenge: Write down every promise to your child this week, and keep it or reschedule it in advance.

advice.scenario: You mention your child's faults casually in front of others.
advice.guidance: In front of others, mention only the good; talk about problems in private. Teens care a lot about how others see them, and when you stand up for them in public, they're more willing to listen at home.
advice.challenge: This week, when you mention your child to others, say only good things.

advice.scenario: You want a later weekend bedtime, and your parent talks it through with you.
advice.guidance: Lay out your reasons and plan: what you'll do with the time and how tomorrow will work. Offering a middle-ground option makes a yes more likely.
advice.challenge: This week, propose a sleep plan you designed yourself.

advice.scenario: You have a screen-time agreement, but sometimes you want more.
advice.guidance: Asking ahead beats sneaking. Explain why you need extra time today and how you'll make up for it. Keeping your word earns you more freedom.
advice.challenge: When you need more screen time this week, ask ahead.

advice.scenario: Your parent has expectations about school and you feel the pressure.
advice.guidance: Your parent is willing to listen, so be specific: which subject, what situation makes you anxious. Set a goal together that feels doable to you.
advice.challenge: Talk to your parent once about school stress and name one specific difficulty.

advice.scenario: You want a sleepover at a friend's and your parent wants details first.
advice.guidance: Offer what they care about up front: who the friend is, whether an adult is home, how to reach you. Good communication makes the next request easier.
advice.challenge: Before your next outing, tell your parent where, with whom and when you'll be back.

advice.scenario: You sometimes forget chores you agreed to.
advice.guidance: Set a phone reminder, or ask to move the chore to a time that suits you. Following through also gives you a stronger case for other freedoms.
advice.challenge: Finish one chore this week without being reminded.

advice.scenario: You're upset but don't want to talk yet.
advice.guidance: You can say "I don't want to talk right now. Maybe later." That way your parent knows you need space rather than feeling shut out.
advice.challenge: Once this week, tell your parent in one sentence how you're feeling.

advice.scenario: You want to buy something fairly expensive.
advice.guidance: Make a mini plan: the price, how much you can pay, and why you want it. When your parent sees you've thought it through, they're more likely to help.
advice.challenge: Write a short plan for something you want to buy and show your parent.

advice.scenario: You disagree with one of your parent's decisions.
advice.guidance: Pick a moment when you're both calm. Say you understand their concern first, then share your view. A calm tone gets your opinion taken more seriously.
advice.challenge: This week, disagree once using "I understand… but I think…"

advice.scenario: You want to stay up all night gaming with friends at the weekend.
advice.guidance: Plan before you ask: when it ends, how you'll catch up on sleep, whether it affects other plans. Offer a middle ground, such as playing until midnight. Keep your word and the next ask gets easier.
advice.challenge: Before making a request this week, write your plan down first.

advice.scenario: You haven't been sleeping well and feel tired during the day.
advice.guidance: Tell your parent, "I haven't been sleeping well," and look at possible causes together: screens before bed, stress, or an irregular routine. If it goes on for a long time, ask your parent about seeing a doctor or talk to the school counsellor.
advice.challenge: No screens for the half hour before bed every night this week.

advice.scenario: You see something online that makes you uncomfortable.
advice.guidance: Close it, then tell your parent or another adult you trust. It isn't your fault, and telling won't get you in trouble; it lets adults help, such as by reporting or blocking it.
advice.challenge: Check the privacy and blocking settings of an app you use with your parent this week.

advice.scenario: You want more screen time, but you haven't kept the current agreement lately.
advice.guidance: Own it first: "I haven't kept to it lately." Then offer to stick to it for a week before talking about changes. Showing it works better than arguing.
advice.challenge: Stop screens at the agreed time every day this week.

advice.scenario: You want to join a club that takes a lot of time.
advice.guidance: Lay out the schedule: how often, how long, and when homework happens. Tell your parent why you like it, and agree on what changes if your grades slip.
advice.challenge: Make a timetable for your activities and study this week.

advice.scenario: You did badly on a test and don't want to tell your parent.
advice.guidance: Telling them yourself goes much better than being found out. Try, "This test didn't go well. I think the reason was…" Your parent is willing to help, and bringing your own ideas makes the talk easier.
advice.challenge: Bring up one result with your parent this week, good or bad.

advice.scenario: Your friends are all going to an event and your parent says they'll think about it.
advice.guidance: Give your parent the details they need: where it is, who's running it, when it ends, how you'll get home. Give them time to think, rather than asking on your way out.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent about any outing at least a day ahead this week.

advice.scenario: A friend wants you to do something you feel isn't right.
advice.guidance: You can just say "I don't want to," no reason needed. If that's hard, "My parent would ask about it" works too, and you can talk with your parent afterwards about how to handle it. Real friends respect your choice.
advice.challenge: Talk with your parent once this week about what to say when friends pressure you.

advice.scenario: You have a crush and aren't sure whether to tell your parent.
advice.guidance: Start at a pace that feels comfortable, maybe with "I've been thinking about someone a lot." Your parent is willing to listen, and talking can help you sort out your feelings. If anyone makes you feel pressured or unsafe, tell your parent or another adult you trust.
advice.challenge: Talk with your parent this week about one relationship that matters to you, a friend or otherwise.

advice.scenario: Chores and homework pile up and you can't get through both.
advice.guidance: Tell your parent early: "I've got loads of homework today. Can I move the chore to tomorrow, or swap it for a quicker one?" Offer an alternative instead of just skipping it.
advice.challenge: If you need to change a chore this week, ask early and offer an alternative.

advice.scenario: You want to learn a life skill, like doing your own laundry.
advice.guidance: Ask your parent to show you once, then take it over. When something goes wrong, like a colour running, try to solve it first, then ask. Looking after yourself is practice for living independently.
advice.challenge: Learn one new household skill this week and do it on your own.

advice.scenario: After an argument with your parent, neither of you is talking.
advice.guidance: Once you've calmed down, try going first: "We both got heated. I'd like to try again." Share how you felt, then listen. Going first isn't losing; it's mending things.
advice.challenge: If you argue this week, make the first move to talk again the same day.

advice.scenario: You're stressed but worried that telling your parent will make them anxious.
advice.guidance: Parents worry more when you carry things alone. Try, "I'm a bit stressed. I don't need you to fix it, I just want to talk." Tell them what kind of support you need.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent once this week which support you need: listening, advice or company.

advice.scenario: You want to earn some money yourself, for example by helping a neighbour.
advice.guidance: Check with your parent whether it's safe and fits around school, and share what you'll do with the money. A plan makes it easier for them to back you.
advice.challenge: Write down one saving goal and plan this week.

advice.scenario: You borrowed money from a friend and haven't paid it back.
advice.guidance: Pay it back soon, or tell your friend when you can. If you can't manage it, talk with your parent, for example about repaying from pocket money over a few weeks. Keeping your word matters with friends and family.
advice.challenge: Pay back what you owe this week, or agree on a date with your friend.

advice.scenario: Your parent comes into your room without knocking.
advice.guidance: Calmly say, "Could you knock before coming in? I'd like a bit of my own space." Respect their space too. Saying what you need works better than slamming the door.
advice.challenge: Make one calm request about privacy this week.

advice.scenario: You take the things your parent does for you for granted.
advice.guidance: Say a specific thank you, like "Thanks for picking me up today." It isn't just manners; it shows you notice what they do, and it makes things better between you.
advice.challenge: Say one specific thank you to your parent each day this week.

advice.scenario: You ask to stay up later and your parent just says "No."
advice.guidance: At a calmer moment, ask "Can you tell me why?" Share your reasons and suggest a one-week trial. Even if the answer is still no, you've been heard.
advice.challenge: At a calm moment this week, ask your parent the reason behind one rule.

advice.scenario: Your phone keeps getting taken away and it feels unfair.
advice.guidance: Go along with it first, then later say "I want to know what would make you comfortable." Ask for the rules to be spelled out, so you know how to avoid it next time.
advice.challenge: Ask your parent to write down the screen rules with you.

advice.scenario: Your parent only notices what you got wrong.
advice.guidance: You can say "I want to improve too, but I need you to see my effort." Show your progress as well, such as corrected homework.
advice.challenge: Show your parent one place where you've improved this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent forbids you from seeing a certain friend.
advice.guidance: Listen to exactly what worries them, then share what makes this friend trustworthy. If they still say no, keep the friendship to public places like school for now.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent one good thing about a friend.

advice.scenario: Whenever you do chores, you're told it isn't good enough.
advice.guidance: Ask exactly how they want it done and ask them to show you once. Afterwards say "I did it the way you showed me" so they see the effort.
advice.challenge: This week, ask your parent to demonstrate how they want one chore done.

advice.scenario: When you're upset, your parent says "Crying won't help."
advice.guidance: Your feelings are normal. Talk to a friend, write them down, or tell a teacher you trust. When things are calm, you can tell your parent: "When I'm upset, I need you to listen first."
advice.challenge: Write down your feelings once this week, or share them with someone you trust.

advice.scenario: You ask for pocket money and your parent says you're too young.
advice.guidance: Suggest something small and concrete: a fixed weekly amount, tracked by you, reviewed together after a month. Show you can handle it.
advice.challenge: Track your spending for a week and show your parent.

advice.scenario: Your parent speaks harshly and you can't help talking back.
advice.guidance: When it heats up, step away to cool down. Later, say which words hurt and how you'd like to be spoken to. If you ever feel unsafe at home, tell a teacher or another adult you trust.
advice.challenge: Once this week, take a deep breath before replying when you want to talk back.

advice.scenario: Your bedtime is much earlier than your classmates' and you feel embarrassed.
advice.guidance: Stick to it for a while to show you can keep rules. Then, at a calm moment, ask, "Could we try half an hour later at weekends?" Small asks are more likely to get a yes than big ones.
advice.challenge: Be in bed on time every day this week, then suggest one small change at the weekend.

advice.scenario: You have so much homework that you can't finish it and still go to bed on time.
advice.guidance: Be specific: "I've got three subjects this week and it'll take about two hours." Ask your parent to help plan the time, rather than staying up in secret. If the workload is always too much, ask your parent to talk to the teacher.
advice.challenge: Write a homework timetable after school every day this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent wants to check your phone whenever they like.
advice.guidance: They're probably worried about your safety. Calmly suggest, "Could we look at it together at a set time instead?" You can also tell them which apps you use. Being open helps them relax.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent one thing you saw or did online this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent says games are a waste of time.
advice.guidance: Invite your parent to watch you play once and tell them what you enjoy, such as teamwork with friends or solving puzzles. Keep to the agreed time so they see games aren't crowding out what matters.
advice.challenge: Invite your parent to watch you play, or talk about a game you like, once this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent signed you up for lots of tutoring and you're exhausted.
advice.guidance: Share feelings and facts together: "I'm only sleeping six hours and can't focus in class." Then suggest something specific, like pausing one class for a month to see what happens to your grades. Results are easier for parents to hear.
advice.challenge: Log your sleep and study time each day this week and show your parent.

advice.scenario: You want to study something your parent thinks is useless.
advice.guidance: Find out what worries them, perhaps that it'll affect core subjects. Explain why you love it and offer a promise, such as keeping core grades at a certain level. You could also start in your free time and prove it works.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent about your interest once this week, and how you'll balance it with school.

advice.scenario: Your parent won't let you sleep over at a friend's.
advice.guidance: Accept the answer this time, then ask, "What would you need to know to feel okay about it?" Suggest your parent meets your friend's parent first, or visit during the day instead. Build trust step by step.
advice.challenge: Introduce a friend or their parent to your parent this week.

advice.scenario: A friend invites you out and you're afraid to ask your parent.
advice.guidance: Prepare before asking: where, who with, when you'll be back, how to reach you. Pick a moment when your parent is in a good mood. If the answer is no, ask why politely and be better prepared next time. Don't go without telling them; that's riskier if something goes wrong.
advice.challenge: Write out the details of any outing before asking your parent this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent tells you to drop everything and do a chore right now.
advice.guidance: If you can stop, go now. If you really can't, calmly say, "I've got five minutes left on this question, then I'll do it." Name a time and stick to it, and your parent will be more willing to give you a little room.
advice.challenge: Each time you're asked to do a chore this week, either go now or name a time and keep it.

advice.scenario: You do lots of chores but never hear a thank you.
advice.guidance: Your effort matters even if no one says so. You could calmly say, "I'd like to hear how I did when I finish." You can also thank your parent first; sometimes adults need the reminder too.
advice.challenge: Thank your parent for one thing they did this week.

advice.scenario: You don't dare show you're unhappy in front of your parent.
advice.guidance: Try writing it first, such as a note or a message: "I've been feeling down and want to talk." If it's hard to say at home, a school counsellor or another adult you trust can listen too.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent how you feel once this week, in a note or message.

advice.scenario: Your parent said hurtful things when angry, and you can't stop thinking about it.
advice.guidance: Your feelings are real. When your parent is calm, you can say, "What you said that day really hurt." If things said at home often leave you scared or feeling unsafe, tell a school counsellor or another adult you trust.
advice.challenge: At a calm moment this week, tell your parent how something they said made you feel.

advice.scenario: Your parent wants a report on every penny you spend, and it annoys you.
advice.guidance: Think of it as practice. You could suggest, "If I keep clear records for a month, can we switch to a weekly check?" Use good records to earn more independence.
advice.challenge: Propose one deal this week that trades good records for more freedom.

advice.scenario: You broke something at home and you're scared of being told off.
advice.guidance: Telling them yourself is better than being found out. Try, "I broke it by accident. I'm sorry, and I can pay for part of it from my pocket money." Owning up shows your honesty. If you're afraid you'll be hurt for telling, talk to an adult you trust first.
advice.challenge: If you make a mistake this week, be the first to say so.

advice.scenario: Your parent criticises you in front of other people.
advice.guidance: Try to stay calm in the moment and not argue back in public. Later, in private: "I know you mean well, but it's embarrassing in front of others. Could you tell me in private?"
advice.challenge: Make one request this week using "Could you tell me in private?"

advice.scenario: Your parent goes back on something they promised you.
advice.guidance: Calmly remind them: "Last week you said…, and I've been looking forward to it." Ask what changed, then find a new plan together. You could suggest writing agreements down from now on.
advice.challenge: Write down one agreement with your parent this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent never asks your opinion before deciding.
advice.guidance: Pick a small decision that affects you, like weekend plans, and offer your view: "Can I share my idea this time?" Starting small helps your parent get used to hearing from you.
advice.challenge: Share your idea on one small decision that affects you this week.

advice.scenario: You often stay up late and nobody really stops you.
advice.guidance: Freedom comes with responsibility. Set your own bedtime and keep your phone out of reach at night. Asking your parent to remind you isn't embarrassing.
advice.challenge: Be in bed by your own bedtime on five days this week.

advice.scenario: No one limits your phone use, but sometimes you can't stop.
advice.guidance: Use your phone's screen-time settings to set your own limit, or ask your parent to agree on rules with you and help you keep them.
advice.challenge: Set yourself a daily screen-time limit this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent rarely asks about school and you tend to procrastinate.
advice.guidance: Make a weekly plan with homework and test dates. You can also ask your parent to check in once a week to help you keep pace.
advice.challenge: Make a study plan this week and check it yourself at the weekend.

advice.scenario: Your parent rarely asks where you're going, and sometimes that worries you too.
advice.guidance: Tell your family where you're going, with whom and when you'll be back. If something happens, they can find you fast. It's for your own protection.
advice.challenge: Each time you go out this week, say where, with whom and when you'll be back.

advice.scenario: Your parent does most of the housework.
advice.guidance: Take on a chore you're good at, like making breakfast or washing up. Your parent will notice the care, and you'll be practising for living on your own.
advice.challenge: Take on one regular chore this week.

advice.scenario: Whenever you're upset, your parent gives you what you want.
advice.guidance: Try making requests only once you've calmed down. Learning to handle disappointment makes school and friendships easier too.
advice.challenge: Once this week, wait until you're calm before asking for something.

advice.scenario: Your parent buys you most things you ask for.
advice.guidance: Wait a week before buying and see whether you still want it. Or try saving up for something you really want.
advice.challenge: Put anything you want to buy this week on a wish list and decide after seven days.

advice.scenario: You sometimes speak to your parent rudely and they don't say anything.
advice.guidance: Silence doesn't mean it doesn't hurt. Try a calmer tone, or say afterwards "Sorry, that came out wrong."
advice.challenge: Once this week, tell your parent "Sorry, that came out wrong."

advice.scenario: You keep saying "One more episode," and suddenly it's past midnight.
advice.guidance: Set an end time and an alarm before you start. When it goes off, stop, no bargaining with yourself. You can also ask your parent to remind you once at that time.
advice.challenge: Set an end alarm before starting any videos each night this week.

advice.scenario: You can't get up in the morning and are often late.
advice.guidance: Pack your bag and lay out your clothes the night before, and put your alarm out of reach of the bed. Your parent could call you once at a set time, but getting up is on you.
advice.challenge: Get your things ready for the next day every night this week.

advice.scenario: You reach for your phone in every spare moment and keep putting off homework.
advice.guidance: Put your phone in another room while you work, or use a 25-minute focus timer and check your phone after each block as a reward. You can also ask your parent to look after it for a while.
advice.challenge: Every day this week, do at least one homework block with your phone in another room.

advice.scenario: You keep comparing yourself with others on social media, and it's bringing you down.
advice.guidance: Notice which accounts leave you feeling worse, and try unfollowing or muting them. Give social media a set time each day. If the low feeling sticks around, talk to your parent, a school counsellor or another adult you trust.
advice.challenge: Unfollow or mute three accounts that make you feel worse this week.

advice.scenario: You always start revising the day before a test.
advice.guidance: As soon as you know a test date, put it in a calendar and mark a start date five days earlier. Ask your parent to remind you that day. Starting a little earlier means far less stress.
advice.challenge: Put every upcoming test in a calendar this week, with a revision start date.

advice.scenario: When you get stuck you just give up, and your parent doesn't ask.
advice.guidance: Give yourself a rule: try for ten minutes, then ask. Ask a classmate, a teacher, or your parent to look things up with you. Write down what you couldn't do and ask the teacher the next day.
advice.challenge: Every day this week, try one hard question for ten minutes before asking for help.

advice.scenario: Friends invite you out very late and your parent says "Up to you."
advice.guidance: Set your own time to be home and tell your parent. If something feels unsafe, "My family wants me back early" is a handy reason. You can also ask your parent to set a time for you; sometimes a rule makes things easier.
advice.challenge: Set your own time to be home for each outing this week, and keep to it.

advice.scenario: You've fallen out with a friend and don't know who to talk to.
advice.guidance: Your parent is willing to listen. Try, "I had a fight with a friend and I'd like your view." Say what happened and what you hope for. You can also take a day to cool off, then talk to your friend.
advice.challenge: Talk to your parent about a friendship once this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent always tidies your room for you.
advice.guidance: Tell your parent, "Let me do it this time." Pick a set time each week to tidy, and put things back after using them. Doing it yourself means you'll know where things are.
advice.challenge: Tidy your room yourself once this week, without help.

advice.scenario: After meals you always leave the table straight away.
advice.guidance: When you get up, take your dishes to the kitchen and ask, "Need any help?" Small things done often become habits, and your parent will notice the care.
advice.challenge: Clear your own dishes after every meal this week.

advice.scenario: When you're in a bad mood you take it out on your family, and your parent lets it go.
advice.guidance: Bad moods are normal, but there are other ways to show them. When you feel about to snap, say, "I need some time alone," then listen to music or breathe slowly. Once you're calm, apologise if you said something harsh.
advice.challenge: When you feel about to snap this week, say "I need some time alone" first.

advice.scenario: You have a worry, and your parent just says "Don't overthink it, just be happy."
advice.guidance: Be clearer: "I know you want me to be happy, but I need you to really listen." Say exactly what happened. If that doesn't work at home, a school counsellor or another adult you trust can help.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent once this week that you need them to really listen.

advice.scenario: You've spent a lot on in-game purchases and your parent hasn't said anything.
advice.guidance: Check how much you've spent this month. Agree on a monthly limit with your parent, and wait for next month once you hit it. You could also turn off one-tap payments so there's a pause before spending.
advice.challenge: Check this month's game spending this week and set a limit.

advice.scenario: You get plenty of pocket money but never know where it goes.
advice.guidance: Track a week of spending in your phone or a notebook, and at the weekend see what was worth it and what you regret. Then try saving a share first and spending the rest.
advice.challenge: Note what you spend, and on what, every day this week.

advice.scenario: You want something expensive and your parent agrees to buy it straight away.
advice.guidance: Offer to pay part of it, for example by saving your pocket money for a month. You value things more when you've helped pay for them.
advice.challenge: Put some money aside this week towards something you want.

advice.scenario: You often half-listen to your parent while looking at your phone.
advice.guidance: When your parent talks, put the phone down, look at them and reply properly. Parents need to feel taken seriously too. Treat them the way you'd like to be treated.
advice.challenge: Put your phone down each time your parent talks to you this week.

advice.scenario: You often forget things you promised your parent.
advice.guidance: Set a phone reminder the moment you agree. If you can't do it, say so early rather than pretending you forgot. Keeping your word is the fastest way to earn your parent's trust.
advice.challenge: Put every promise to your parent in your phone this week, and keep it.

advice.scenario: Nobody at home cares when you go to bed or says good night.
advice.guidance: Build your own wind-down routine, like getting ready at a set time and listening to music. You can also say good night first; small greetings bring people closer.
advice.challenge: Say good night to your family every night this week.

advice.scenario: You spend most evenings alone in your room on your phone.
advice.guidance: Invite someone at home to watch a video you like or play a game with you. Sharing your world is a start to being known.
advice.challenge: Invite your parent to watch or play something you like this week.

advice.scenario: It feels like nobody cares about your schoolwork.
advice.guidance: Share a test or homework result with your parent yourself. You can also ask a teacher for help; many people at school want to support you.
advice.challenge: Share one thing from school with your parent this week.

advice.scenario: Nobody at home asks where you're going.
advice.guidance: Even if no one asks, send a message saying where you are. It keeps you safe and gives your family a chance to care.
advice.challenge: Each time you go out this week, send your family a message.

advice.scenario: Everyone at home does their own thing and rarely does anything together.
advice.guidance: Suggest cooking a meal or tidying up together. Doing something side by side is an easier way to start talking than sitting down for a chat.
advice.challenge: Suggest one thing the whole family can do together this week.

advice.scenario: When you're unhappy, it feels like no one notices.
advice.guidance: Your feelings matter. Try telling someone at home "I've been feeling down lately." If that's hard at home, talk to the school counsellor or another adult you trust.
advice.challenge: Tell one person you trust how you've been feeling this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent gives you money but never asks what it's for.
advice.guidance: Tell them what you bought and why you like it. It's an easy way to let them into your interests.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent about something you bought this week.

advice.scenario: When you talk, your parent often seems distracted.
advice.guidance: Pick a time when they aren't busy and start with "Can you give me five minutes? I want to tell you something." Asking clearly makes it easier to be heard.
advice.challenge: Start one conversation this week with "Can you give me five minutes?"

advice.scenario: Nobody at home reminds you, so you often stay up very late.
advice.guidance: Choose your own bedtime and set a phone reminder to start winding down. Enough sleep makes school and your mood a lot better.
advice.challenge: Start getting ready for bed when the reminder goes off every night this week.

advice.scenario: You're home alone at night and feel scared or can't sleep.
advice.guidance: Tell your parent how it feels: "I get scared at home alone at night." Work out a plan together, such as a set time to call, or a relative who can come over. If you often feel unsafe, tell a school counsellor or another adult you trust.
advice.challenge: Agree on a way to reach your parent in the evenings this week.

advice.scenario: You met someone online who wants to meet you alone.
advice.guidance: Tell your parent or a trusted adult first, and never meet someone from online on your own. A real friend will understand that an adult needs to know. If they ask you to keep it secret or pressure you, that's a warning sign: tell an adult straight away.
advice.challenge: Tell your parent or a trusted adult who you talk to online this week.

advice.scenario: You use your phone to fill lonely time, but it leaves you feeling emptier.
advice.guidance: Swap some screen time for something else: exercise, drawing or seeing friends. You could also invite someone at home for a walk or a snack. If loneliness keeps weighing on you, talk to the school counsellor.
advice.challenge: Swap half an hour of screen time for something else each day this week.

advice.scenario: School needs a parent's signature or attendance, but your parent keeps forgetting.
advice.guidance: Tell your parent a few days ahead and remind them the day before, perhaps leaving the note where they're sure to see it. If it still doesn't work, tell your teacher; they can help find a way.
advice.challenge: Write anything school needs from your parent on a note and hand it to them this week.

advice.scenario: Your grades are slipping and no one has noticed.
advice.guidance: Look for the cause first: which subject, and since when. Ask a teacher for advice, or study with a classmate. Also try telling your parent, "My grades have dropped a bit and I want to improve," so they have a chance to support you.
advice.challenge: Ask a teacher or classmate for help with schoolwork once this week.

advice.scenario: You're being picked on at school and feel no one at home can help.
advice.guidance: It isn't your fault, and you don't have to face it alone. Tell a teacher, the school counsellor or another adult you trust what happened and when. Try telling your parent too; they may want to help more than you think.
advice.challenge: Tell a teacher or an adult you trust what has been happening this week.

advice.scenario: You want to invite friends over but don't know if your parent will agree.
advice.guidance: Just ask: "Can two friends come over on Saturday afternoon? We'll tidy up." Being clear about the time and numbers makes a yes easier, and it's a good chance for your parent to meet your friends.
advice.challenge: Introduce one of your friends to your parent this week.

advice.scenario: Home is messy and nobody tidies up.
advice.guidance: Start with your own space, like your room or desk. You could also suggest, "Let's spend twenty minutes tidying the living room together this weekend." When one person starts, others often join in.
advice.challenge: Spend ten minutes tidying your own space each day this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent gets home late and you often sort out your own meals.
advice.guidance: Learn a few simple, safe meals, like boiled eggs or sandwiches, and take care with the hob. You could also suggest cooking a few days' meals together at the weekend. If there's often no food at home, tell your parent or a trusted adult at school.
advice.challenge: Learn to make one simple dish this week.

advice.scenario: You want your parent's attention but don't know how to ask.
advice.guidance: Say it directly: "I'd like to do something with you. Are you free tonight?" A specific request gets a better response than "You never pay attention to me." If tonight doesn't work, ask when would.
advice.challenge: Ask your parent for one specific bit of time together this week.

advice.scenario: You feel there's no one you can talk to.
advice.guidance: Think of people you trust: a relative, a teacher, the school counsellor, a friend's parent. Start by telling one of them a little. If you feel very low or unsafe, tell an adult straight away.
advice.challenge: Write down three people you trust and could talk to this week.

advice.scenario: You did something you're proud of, and there's no one to share it with.
advice.guidance: Tell your parent yourself: "I did something today and I want to tell you!" They may just not have noticed; it doesn't mean they don't care. Share it with a friend or teacher too, and celebrate yourself.
advice.challenge: Share one thing that made you happy with your parent this week.

advice.scenario: You need school supplies but feel awkward asking for money.
advice.guidance: Write a list of what you need, roughly how much, and when, and give it to your parent. A clear request is easier to say yes to. You could also suggest a fixed monthly allowance.
advice.challenge: Give your parent a list of what you need this week.

advice.scenario: You have some pocket money but don't know how to save it.
advice.guidance: Each time you get money, put a small share aside, say a tenth, in one place. Pick a goal; watching it grow feels good. You can also ask your parent or a teacher to show you how to keep track.
advice.challenge: Save part of any money you get this week before spending.

advice.scenario: Your parent talks to you coldly, and you've started doing the same.
advice.guidance: Try a gentle line first, like "Was work tiring today?" You can't control your parent's tone, but you can choose yours. Sometimes a small kindness softens the other person too.
advice.challenge: Greet your parent first each day this week.

advice.scenario: Your parent is always on calls or working when you're around, and you feel ignored.
advice.guidance: At a time they're not busy, say, "I'd like a little time each day when we really talk, like at dinner." Naming a specific time works better than complaining.
advice.challenge: Agree on a daily time to talk with your parent this week.
